title: A church news post, opened from the email without the app
question: Someone taps Read the post in the What's Next email on a computer, or on a phone without the app. Each sketch shows a window at the left and a phone at the right. Which way should the post sit?

options.label: A bulletin page on the desk
options.thesis: The post as the app sets it, on a white page lying on sand, with the church's name above and the app line under it.
materials: the post's navy rule and sand foot
options.viewport: Good Shepherd with the mark at the top left of a sand stage; a white page centred with the post (navy rule, date block, title, picture, lead); under the page a quiet caption: also in the app, ask the church office. On a phone the page runs edge to edge.
options.risk: Two sands meet at the page's foot, so the post's own sand foot needs a hairline to read as the end.

options.label: The app strip at the top
options.thesis: A sand strip across the top says who it's from and that it's in the app; under it the post is a plain white page.
options.viewport: A sand strip across the top: the mark and Good Shepherd at the left, and 'This post is also in the Good Shepherd app. Ask the church office how to get it.' at the right; then the post in a 680px column on white, its sand foot across the window.
options.risk: A strip at the top looks like an app banner and may be read past.

options.label: A navy band, like the app's masthead
options.thesis: A navy band with the mark and 'Church news' opens the page as the app's masthead would; the app line closes the sand foot.
materials: sand foot carrying the app line
options.viewport: A short navy band across the top: the white mark, Good Shepherd, and 'Church news' in beige; then the post in a 680px column on white; its sand foot says who posted it and, on a second line, that it's also in the app.
options.risk: The navy band and the post's own navy rule sit close together; the band must stay short.
